record.title: System One decision models show lower wrong-pick rates on a constructed legal-authority abstention test
record.summary: A University at Albany preprint compares four System One decision models with six generative language models on the CaseHOLD legal-reasoning benchmark. In a constructed abstention condition, the authors replace the correct holding with a similar real holding in 1,670 of 5,314 test items and add a “none” option. They report wrong-pick rates of 37.8–85.6% for generative models and 30.1–60.8% for decision models; the most cautious decision model also abstains on 26.2% of items where the correct holding remains. An agreement gate between a decision model and a generative model reportedly halves wrong citations on a held-out split. These are author-reported results from one English-language U.S. case-law task, not independent reproduction or evidence of legal reliability in practice.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that when the correct holding is replaced by a similar real holding, six generative models select a wrong holding in 37.8–85.6% of affected test items, while four decision models do so in 30.1–60.8%.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that the most cautious decision model has a 30.1% wrong-pick rate on affected items and falsely abstains on 26.2% of items where the correct holding remains.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On a held-out split, the authors report that accepting a generative model answer only when a decision model agrees halves wrong citations for the strongest tested generative model.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The results do not establish practical legal reliability, citation correctness, or transfer beyond this English U.S. CaseHOLD task and constructed missing-holding condition.

evidence_gaps.description: Reported metrics and the agreement gate have not been independently recomputed or reproduced in this review.

The constructed absence condition replaces a holding with a similar real holding and does not test other common gaps such as overruled authority, wrong jurisdiction, nonexistent cases, or retrieved evidence that does not support a proposition.
The relative cost assigned to a wrong citation versus an unnecessary human review is illustrative; it varies by legal setting and user.

brief.importance_rationale: If these results transfer to legal authority checks, selective abstention could reduce costly unsupported citations at relatively low inference cost. Consequence is meaningful for tool design and evaluation, but evidence is one author-run English U.S. CaseHOLD task using a constructed missing-holding condition; practical legal reliability and generalization are not established.
limitations: This is a single author-run preprint accepted to a workshop; no independent reproduction was performed.
The test uses English-language U.S. case law and a constructed missing-holding condition, not live legal research workflows.
Model agreement is not proof that a citation supports a proposition; source reading and legal verification remain necessary.
The wrong-citation versus manual-review cost ratio is illustrative and user-specific.
The paper states that contamination checks cannot rule out that closed models saw some public passages during training.
brief.summary: A University at Albany preprint compares four System One decision models with six generative language models on the CaseHOLD legal-reasoning benchmark. In a constructed abstention condition, the authors replace the correct holding with a similar real holding in 1,670 of 5,314 test items and add a “none” option. They report wrong-pick rates of 37.8–85.6% for generative models and 30.1–60.8% for decision models; the most cautious decision model also abstains on 26.2% of items where the correct holding remains. An agreement gate between a decision model and a generative model reportedly halves wrong citations on a held-out split. These are author-reported results from one English-language U.S. case-law task, not independent reproduction or evidence of legal reliability in practice.

technical.claimed_result: On the full 5,314-item CaseHOLD test set, the authors report wrong-pick rates of 37.8–85.6% for six generative models and 30.1–60.8% for four decision models when the correct holding was removed from 1,670 items. The most cautious decision model reports a 30.1% wrong-pick rate and a 26.2% false-abstention rate. A decision-model agreement gate reportedly halves wrong citations for the strongest generative model on a 70% held-out split. On original CaseHOLD, one decision model reports 88.1% accuracy at about 1/55 the cost of the best generative model’s 88.2%.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv preprint and linked public repository establish that the study, constructed benchmark condition, prompts, saved per-item outputs and analysis scripts were released. The reported accuracy, abstention, cost and agreement-gate effects are author-reported and were not independently reproduced in this review.
technical.mechanism: System One decision models return probabilities over a closed set of candidate holdings, including a none-of-these option. The study combines such a model with a generative model through an agreement gate that accepts only matching answers and sends disagreements for review.
technical.regime: One English-language U.S. legal holding-selection task built from public court opinions; one prompt per model type; four decision models and six generative models available in October 2026. Missing authority is simulated by replacing a correct holding with a similar real holding from another case.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares ten model versions on the same CaseHOLD test items with fixed short prompts, reports bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests, and reserves a random 30% of items to tune combination thresholds before reporting on the remaining 70%. No independent reproduction, live retrieval test or legal-practice benchmark was performed.

brief.title: System One decision models show lower wrong-pick rates on a constructed legal-authority abstention test
brief.why_it_matters: A low-cost abstention check could help identify unsupported authority claims before they reach legal workflows, and the study shows why wrong citations and unnecessary review should be measured separately. The result is bounded to one constructed CaseHOLD condition; it does not establish that model agreement makes a citation correct, or that the gains transfer to real retrieval, overruled cases, jurisdiction mismatch or other legal systems.
